title: The Law versus Grace and the Power of Baptism
english: … people of Antioch and to the whole world. So it is unfitting for you to teach others these things, when you yourself have stopped observing them and have abolished them by your own decree.

On Galatians 2:19–20: The law is about bodily things, about doing them and enjoying them: eat this, do not eat that, keep the Sabbath, be circumcised. Grace does not want you to earn approval by such things. So, he says, I have died to them. What need have I of the law? “It is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me.” While I lived for myself, I was under the law. But since Christ lives in me, and he is no longer under the law but in the heavens at the Father’s right hand, I do not set aside the one who lives in me. “And the life I now live in the flesh, I live by faith”, since I believe in the Son of God. If the Son of God, in whom I believe, is at the Father’s right hand, then my citizenship is in the heavens. The law kept its observances among the things of earth. So I am not subject to the law.

On Galatians 3:19–22: The law was a heavier burden, and that is why it was called a ministry of death (2 Corinthians 3:7). Then how, he asks, was it added because of transgressions? Put briefly, it is like this. Before the law, the human mind, together with the flesh, served sin and was fond of evil. When the law was given, the mind was taught, but the flesh was still held captive. Now, a man who does not know that sin is sin takes up impiety as if it were piety and gives himself to it all the more eagerly. But a man who knows that it is evil gains at least this much: he is aware that he is transgressing, and he longs to obey God. That is why the law was given. “A law that could give life” means this: if a law was given, it was not given, he says, against the promises of God; but neither could it keep its hold for ever.
On Galatians 3:23: Even if the law achieved nothing else, it did give people the knowledge of God. And knowing God made them ready to receive grace.

On Galatians 3:27–28: It is not keeping the law, he says, that makes Jews who have believed better than those who came from the Gentiles. It is the power of baptism, which lets us put on Christ, that makes grace common to all alike: barbarians, Greeks, Jews, female and male. He did not add “female and male” idly, since, as far as the wording goes, “one” was what the point at hand required. Rather, if baptism gathers male and female, different as they are, into one grace, how much more Greek and Jew!

On Galatians 4:8–10: Now he wants to show that once grace has come, anyone who still claims to keep Sabbaths, new moons and feasts by the law is as good as worshipping the elements as idols, the elements he served when he was a pagan. He is a slave again, only in another form. And he does not …

title: The Nature of Allegory and Prophecy
english: … keep the law, for the law has come to an end. When he calls the elements “beggarly”, he is not accusing them of being evil. He means that they cannot make anyone rich and are not enough for true piety.

On Galatians 4:12: Do not think, he says, that I have some other grievance against you and that this is why I rebuke you. For the pain he feels keeps forcing him to change the form of his speech: now he reproves, now he encourages, at one moment he accuses, at another he laments. So here he teaches them that what he writes, he writes out of love. “You have done me no wrong,” he says; on the contrary, I was treated with care, with the greatest care of all.

On Galatians 4:15–18: “What, then, was the blessedness?” This stands for “there was none.” Or take it this way: which is blessed, keeping the law or living by faith? He had said that those men do not want to follow your example, which would give them the perfection of faith without keeping the law; they want you to follow theirs. So he went on to say: I am not saying this because I grudge them anything. I wish they too had become perfect by making use of faith; then nothing would stop them from being taken as models and from imitating us. As for you, act in a way that makes you worth following, so that everyone may imitate you. Do not become like this only when I come, out of respect for me; correct yourselves even when I am not with you.

On Galatians 4:23–24: Here he uses the word loosely, not in the proper sense of allegory. Allegory does not stay with what is actually said. It brings in something else, which shows through the sequence of thoughts woven into the text. An example is “Let him kiss me with the kisses of his mouth” in the Song of Songs (Song of Solomon 1:2). There it is not really a kiss, or hair, or a belly, or thighs, or anything of the kind; one thing is conveyed by means of another, and that is allegory properly so called. Here, though, the history is accepted as true, and it is also shown to be a type of what was to come. So what he now calls allegory is prophecy by deeds. Some prophecies are given by words alone, like “Behold, the virgin shall conceive in the womb” (Isaiah 7:14). Some are given by deeds alone, as when “Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness” (John 3:14). And some are given by deeds and words together, like the command to Jeremiah: “Take a new loincloth and put it on. Then bury it by the Euphrates.” And when time had rotted it and eaten it away, “take it,” he says, “from there” (Jeremiah 13:1–7). Up to this point the prophecy is in deeds; what follows is in words as well: in this way I too wrapped the sons of Israel around me (Jeremiah 13:11), and in this way I helped them; in this way I am leading them away captive to Babylon, and when they have rotted and decayed there I will bring them back and restore them. title: Allegorical Interpretation of Law and Promise
english: On Galatians 4:25: He did not mention Mount Sinai idly. He did it because the Hagarenes, the descendants of Ishmael, hold the desert that runs right up to Mount Sinai. It was on Sinai that the law was given, the law that bears children for slavery. The tablets given on Mount Sinai were carried about in Israel, moved again and again from place to place, and at last set up in Jerusalem. That is why he added: “It corresponds to the present Jerusalem, for she is in slavery with her children.” Wherever there is a promise of land, with property and marriage and all the business of human life, slavery follows. But where there is release from earthly cares and ties, and our citizenship is in heaven, freedom comes from that citizenship itself.

On Galatians 5:17: People ask why, while he is drawing them away from the law, he speaks about sin. The reason is that the law told them to enjoy plenty. That stirs up desire, and desire, once it cannot be held back, leads on to sin. So whenever he mentioned the law, he mentioned sin as well. In the letter to the Romans too, when he speaks of the law, he also brings in the correction that came through the Lord: “For those who live according to the flesh cannot please God” (Romans 8:8). Why, then, were feasting and eating allowed at all? Because they would not have made progress in keeping away from evils everyone admits to be evils, unless they had been allowed to eat and drink. The lawgiver knew, of course, that people who live in plenty cannot master their pleasures. For the time being, though, he wanted to train the mind, so that it would know what is good, what is evil and what is godly. He foresaw that someone was coming who would add what the law lacked: I mean not walking according to the flesh, as Paul puts it (Romans 8:4).

On Galatians 6:7–8: Here he makes it plain that many were spending their money unwisely. They supplied the men who were urging them to keep the law and gave nothing to those who preached Paul’s teaching. That is why he says, “He who sows to his own flesh”; for anyone subject to the law lives among the things of the flesh. So whoever supports a man who teaches such things is sowing to the flesh and nothing more.

On Galatians 6:14–15: He did not want to be thought to be championing uncircumcision against circumcision, and so hand his opponents an excuse to slander him. So he very aptly added the last words: neither circumcision counts for anything nor uncircumcision, and he spoke instead of a new creation. Of this he says elsewhere: “If anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation” (2 Corinthians 5:17). If you are a new creation, he says, do not put yourself under the law. Whoever lives by the law lives in the world, but whoever lives in Christ has his citizenship in heaven. So “the world has been crucified to me, and I to the world.”
